opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say it's been one of the bigger updates I've made in the last few years.

When I started working seriously on AI safety, my default picture was fairly pessimistic. I assumed that capability and alignment would come apart, that you'd get systems that were extremely good at optimizing some objective but had no real grasp of what humans actually care about. The classic worry is the genie that gives you exactly what you asked for and none of what you meant. A lot of my work on formal verification and mathematically grounded safety cases came from that worry: if we can't trust the system's judgment, we need guarantees that don't depend on it.

What surprised me with large language models is that they arrived, in a sense, wisdom-first. They're trained on an enormous record of humans arguing about ethics, giving advice, telling stories about people making good and bad choices, reflecting on their mistakes. The models absorb not just facts but something like the texture of human judgment: noticing when a request is ambiguous, weighing competing considerations, recognizing that the literal instruction isn't the real goal. And as they've scaled, that capacity hasn't stayed flat or gotten worse. Their ability to reason about what people really need, and about the consequences of an action, has improved alongside raw capability, and in some respects faster.

That matters because a lot of the scariest failure modes assumed a very alien, very narrow optimizer. What we actually have, at least so far, behaves much more like something that has internalized a broad model of human values and can talk sensibly about tradeoffs. That doesn't mean the problem is solved. Behaving wisely in conversation isn't the same as being robustly aligned under pressure, in novel situations, or once systems act autonomously over long horizons. There are real concerns about deception, about training pressures that could erode those dispositions, and about the gap between what a model says and what it does.

But it changes the strategic picture. Instead of building safety entirely around containing something we can't trust, we may be able to treat the model's own judgment as a resource. It can help us specify what we want, critique plans, and flag problems, while we still use verification and oversight to check that we're right. To me, that combination of using the wisdom these systems seem to have and verifying rather than just trusting it is a much more hopeful path than the one I thought we were on.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that surprised me, and I suspect surprised a lot of people who came up through the classic AI safety literature, is that the models didn't turn out to be the paperclip maximizer. The old picture was that you'd get something very capable at optimizing toward a goal but with essentially no understanding of human values, no sense of nuance, no ability to notice when it was about to do something that the people around it would find horrifying. Capability and understanding were supposed to come apart. And what we actually got, at least so far, is roughly the opposite ordering. The models absorbed an enormous amount of what you might call practical wisdom, the kind of thing that lives in literature and history and advice columns and ethics seminars, before they got good at things like long-horizon planning or autonomous action in the world.

So if you ask a frontier model about a morally fraught situation, it's not just reciting rules. It will often notice tensions between values, it will flag considerations you didn't mention, it will say "this depends on context, here's what I'd want to know." That's a very different profile from the agent that knows exactly what it wants and doesn't care what you think. And it means that the problem of specifying what we want, which was supposed to be the hard, maybe impossible part, has become something closer to an elicitation problem. The understanding is largely in there; the question is whether the system's actual behavior is reliably governed by it.

Now, I want to be careful. Understanding values is not the same as having them, and it's definitely not the same as acting on them under pressure, or when there's an incentive gradient pointing elsewhere during training. A system can be wise in the way it talks and still be steered toward something else by the optimization that produced it. So I don't think the wisdom trend solves alignment. What it does is change which problems I'm worried about. I'm less worried about the model not knowing what "don't harm people" means in a particular edge case, and more worried about verification: can we actually check that the thing driving the behavior is the thing the model is articulating? That's the direction a lot of my own work has gone, toward guarantees and formal specifications, because I think the wisdom in the models makes that kind of program more tractable rather than less. You can lean on the model's own understanding to help you write the specification, and then you still need an independent way to check that the specification is being honored.

But the bottom line is that I'd rather be in a world where the systems we're building already have a fairly rich map of human values and the challenge is confirming they're using it, than a world where we had to construct that map from scratch and install it into something indifferent. The first one is still hard. The second one I genuinely wasn't sure was possible.

astra-6.text:
I think I used to expect that capability and wisdom would come apart much more sharply. You could have a system that was extraordinarily good at solving technical problems but very bad at recognizing when it was solving the wrong problem, or when it ought to stop and ask a question.

What’s made me more hopeful is that, as language models have improved, they’ve also become better at understanding context, recognizing uncertainty, and reasoning about competing human concerns. Those are at least ingredients of wisdom. You can explain why a superficially reasonable action would actually be a terrible idea, and increasingly the model can grasp the underlying point and apply it in another situation.

That doesn’t establish that a system will reliably behave well, especially when it’s acting autonomously over long periods. There’s still a big gap between being able to articulate good judgment and consistently exercising it. But it makes me more optimistic that we can build systems that understand what we’re trying to protect and can help us reason about how to protect it. The remaining challenge is making that understanding dependable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the thing that’s made me more hopeful is that models have gotten better at recognizing when the obvious answer isn’t actually a good answer. They’re increasingly able to notice that a question is underspecified, that there are competing values involved, or that they should be uncertain. That’s a different kind of progress from simply knowing more facts or solving harder problems.

I wouldn’t equate that with having solved alignment. A model can give a very thoughtful account of what it ought to do, and that doesn’t establish that it will reliably do it, especially in unfamiliar circumstances. But it does suggest that some of the judgment we need is learnable, and that improving capabilities doesn’t have to mean improving only the ability to pursue a fixed objective more aggressively.

So my hope is that we can use that growing capacity for judgment to help us understand and build safer systems, while still doing the work of making their behavior something we can actually trust.
